standard_text: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns of association between two quantitative variables. Describe patterns such as clustering, outliers, positive or negative association, linear association, and nonlinear association.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to construct scatter plots from two-variable data and describe what they see: positive, negative, or no association, linear or nonlinear form, and local features like clusters and outliers. The on-grade work moves from naming the direction of the drift, to judging straight versus curved, to spotting clusters and lone points, and finally to building a plot from a table and describing it in the variables' own words. Students who stall here usually cannot yet plot an ordered pair reliably or read how one quantity changes with another in a table. Intervention should rebuild those grades 5 and 6 foundations, then the grade 7 skills of reading proportional graphs point by point and describing a dot plot's shape and stray values, before returning to scatter plots.

steps.rationale: Direction is the first observable judgment a scatter plot supports, and the Below-proficiency band asks for exactly it: name the association as positive, negative, or none. It comes first because every later description is built on knowing which way the cloud drifts.

Form is the second axis of description the standard names by hand -- linear versus nonlinear. It sits after direction because a student must first see the drift before deciding whether that drift follows a straight line or a curve.

Clustering and outliers are local features the standard lists explicitly. They form a separate step from direction and form because they describe WHERE the points sit -- bunched or lone -- not which way the data trends.

The Approaching-proficiency band asks students to identify MORE THAN ONE characteristic at once. This synthesis step combines direction, form, and any cluster or outlier into a single full description of the plot.

The At-proficiency heart of the standard: construct a scatter plot from a data table and interpret the pattern IN CONTEXT, stating how the response variable changes as the explanatory variable increases, using the real variable names.

The Above-proficiency band: analyze and critique a described pattern, create a scatter plot to match given descriptors, and separate correlation from causation -- refusing to claim one variable causes the other from association alone.

skills.name: Plot and name ordered pairs in the first quadrant

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot a point from an ordered pair (x, y), moving right for the first number and up for the second, and read the pair for a plotted point.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot (2, 6), how far right and how far up do you move?

skills.i_do_script: An ordered pair is a set of walking directions, and the order is fixed: right first, then up. Watch me plot (3, 5): I start at the corner where the axes meet, walk right 3, then walk up 5, and put my dot there. To read a dot that sits 4 right and 2 up, I write (4, 2), x first, y second. The trap is swapping the numbers: (3, 5) and (5, 3) land on two different dots, and I can prove it by walking both paths on the grid.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the coordinates, moving up for the first number and right for the second
canonical_error.example: Plots (3, 5) by going right 5 and up 3, landing at (5, 3)
canonical_error.why: The student has not fixed the order of the pair. The first number is always the horizontal move and the second is always the vertical move, so reversing them plots a different point.

skills.item_template: An ordered pair to plot, or a point described as so many right and so many up to name as a pair. Whole numbers 0 to 10. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: To plot (2, 7), how far right and how far up do you move?
sample_items.answer: Right 2, up 7

sample_items.stem: A dot is 6 right and 1 up. Write its ordered pair.
Do (4, 9) and (9, 4) name the same point?
sample_items.answer: No, order matters, they are different points

sample_items.stem: Which point is farther right: (8, 2) or (3, 9)?
sample_items.answer: (8, 2), its x-coordinate 8 is larger

sample_items.stem: Which point is higher up: (8, 2) or (3, 9)?
sample_items.answer: (3, 9), its y-coordinate 9 is larger

sample_items.stem: For (5, 0), how far up do you move?
sample_items.answer: 0, the point sits on the x-axis

sample_items.stem: For (0, 4), how far right do you move?
sample_items.answer: 0, the point sits on the y-axis

sample_items.stem: A dot is 3 right and 3 up. Write its ordered pair.

redirect_script.stop: Which number moves you right, the first or the second?
redirect_script.prompt: Walk both orders on the grid with your finger and see that they land on two different dots. Say 'right, then up' as you point to each number before you place the dot.
redirect_script.praise: You moved right for the first number and up for the second, that is exactly how an ordered pair works.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that give a point's position: right first, then up.
The first number in a pair; how far right the point sits.
The second number in a pair; how far up the point sits.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 5 coordinate grids by walking points on a floor grid or large graph paper, right first and then up.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a 0 to 6 grid. Plot (4, 2) and (2, 4) as two dots.
Same two numbers made both dots. Why are they in different spots?
(4, 2) is right 4 then up 2. (2, 4) is right 2 then up 4. The order of the walk decides where the dot lands.
If a student puts both dots in one spot, ask which number moved them right for each pair.
Your turn: plot (5, 1) and (1, 5) and tell me how they differ.

skills.name: Describe how one quantity changes with another from a two-variable table

prerequisite_skill.description: Given a table of two related quantities, tell which variable depends on the other and describe whether the dependent quantity increases or decreases as the independent quantity increases.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A table shows hours worked 1, 2, 3 and pay 9, 18, 27. As hours go up, what does pay do?

skills.i_do_script: A two-column table tells a story about two quantities that change together, and I read it one row at a time. Watch this table: hours worked 1, 2, 3, 4 and pay 9, 18, 27, 36. Hours is the quantity I control, so it is the independent variable, and pay depends on hours, so pay is the dependent variable. Reading down the rows, as hours climb 1, 2, 3, 4, pay climbs 9, 18, 27, 36. So I say the relationship in a sentence: as hours worked increase, pay increases. I always read the rows in order of the independent variable before I decide.

canonical_error.pattern: Describes the change by reading rows in whatever order they are listed instead of ordering by the independent variable
canonical_error.example: For rows (3, 12), (1, 4), (2, 8) reads the second column as 12, 4, 8 and says there is no pattern
canonical_error.why: The question is how the dependent quantity changes AS the independent quantity increases, so the rows must be put in order of the independent variable first. List order is just the order someone wrote them down.

skills.item_template: A small table of two related quantities (3 to 5 rows, whole numbers). Student names the independent and dependent variable or states whether the second quantity increases or decreases as the first increases. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Hours worked: 1, 2, 3. Pay: 9, 18, 27. As hours increase, what does pay do?
sample_items.answer: Pay increases (9, 18, 27)

sample_items.stem: Weeks: 1, 2, 3, 4. Money left: 40, 30, 20, 10. As weeks increase, what does money left do?
sample_items.answer: Money left decreases (40, 30, 20, 10)

sample_items.stem: In the hours and pay table, which quantity depends on the other?
sample_items.answer: Pay depends on hours worked, so pay is the dependent variable

sample_items.stem: Rows out of order: (3, 12), (1, 4), (2, 8). Put them in order of the first quantity and say what the second does.
sample_items.answer: Ordered: (1, 4), (2, 8), (3, 12). The second quantity increases

sample_items.stem: Rows: (4, 5), (2, 9), (3, 7). Order by the first quantity. Does the second rise or fall?
sample_items.answer: Ordered: (2, 9), (3, 7), (4, 5). It falls

sample_items.stem: Bags: 1, 2, 3. Apples: 6, 12, 18. How many apples does each new bag add?
sample_items.answer: 6 apples per bag

sample_items.stem: Why must you order the rows before deciding if the second quantity goes up or down?
sample_items.answer: Because the change is described as the first quantity increases, so the first quantity must be in order

sample_items.stem: Minutes: 5, 10, 15. Water in tub (gallons): 30, 20, 10. As minutes increase, what does the water do?
sample_items.answer: It decreases, the tub is draining

redirect_script.stop: Are the rows in order of the first quantity yet?
redirect_script.prompt: Line the rows up from smallest to largest first quantity, then read the second column top to bottom and say whether it climbs or falls.
redirect_script.praise: You ordered the rows first and then read the change, that is how you see the real relationship.

vocabulary.definition: The quantity you choose or control; the one you read in order.
The quantity that responds; its value depends on the independent variable.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 6 tables of related quantities using a simple in-out machine picture with one rule.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a table: weeks 1, 2, 3, 4 in one column and money left 40, 30, 20, 10 in the other. Sketch a bar for each money value so the bars step down.
Which quantity depends on the other? What do the bars do as the weeks go by?
Money left depends on weeks, and the bars shrink 40, 30, 20, 10. As weeks increase, money left decreases by 10 each week.
If a student reads the money column out of row order, have them number the rows by weeks first.
Your turn: hours 1, 2, 3 and miles 4, 8, 12. Say the relationship in one sentence.

skills.name: Graph a proportional relationship and interpret points in context

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot points from a proportional table, see that they form a straight line through the origin, and explain what a point (x, y) means in the situation.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Apples cost 3 dollars per pound. On the graph of this relationship, what does the point (4, 12) mean?

skills.i_do_script: In grade 7 we graphed relationships where every point follows one steady rule. Watch: apples cost 3 dollars per pound, so I build the table (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12) and plot each pair. The dots line up on a straight line that passes through (0, 0), because 0 pounds cost 0 dollars. Each point is a sentence: (4, 12) says 4 pounds cost 12 dollars, and (1, 3) names the unit rate, 3 dollars for 1 pound. This is the cleanest picture of two quantities moving together, and a scatter plot is the messy real-data version of the same idea.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads a point as two separate numbers instead of one pair with a meaning in context
canonical_error.example: For the point (4, 12) on the apples graph says 'there are 4 dollars and 12 pounds' or cannot say what the point means
canonical_error.why: A point on the graph is one fact about the situation: the x-value and y-value belong to the same purchase. The student must attach x to its variable and y to its variable, in order, before reading the meaning.

skills.item_template: A proportional situation with a whole-number unit rate (2 to 9). Student completes or plots the table, states the meaning of a point, names the unit rate point, or checks whether a table is proportional. Short response.

sample_items.stem: Apples cost 3 dollars per pound. What does the point (4, 12) on the graph mean?
sample_items.answer: 4 pounds of apples cost 12 dollars

sample_items.stem: On the apples graph (3 dollars per pound), which point shows the unit rate?
sample_items.answer: (1, 3), 1 pound costs 3 dollars

sample_items.stem: A biker rides 8 miles each hour. Complete the pair: (3, ?)
sample_items.answer: (3, 24), 3 hours is 24 miles

sample_items.stem: Does the graph of a proportional relationship pass through (0, 0)? Why?
sample_items.answer: Yes, 0 of the first quantity gives 0 of the second

sample_items.stem: Table: (1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15). Is it proportional? What is the unit rate?
sample_items.answer: Yes, y is always 5 times x, unit rate 5

sample_items.stem: Table: (1, 4), (2, 7), (3, 10). Is it proportional?
sample_items.answer: No, 4/1, 7/2, 10/3 are not equal, and the line would not pass through (0, 0)

sample_items.stem: A car goes 60 miles in 1 hour at a steady speed. What point shows the distance after 2 hours?
On a graph of pounds vs cost, point A is (2, 8) and point B is (5, 20). Which purchase cost more?
sample_items.answer: Point B, 20 dollars for 5 pounds

redirect_script.stop: What does the x of that point stand for, and what does the y stand for?
redirect_script.prompt: Say the point as a sentence using the axis labels: x pounds cost y dollars. The two numbers describe one purchase together, not two separate things.
redirect_script.praise: You read the point as one fact about the situation, that is interpreting the graph.

vocabulary.definition: Two quantities where one is always the same multiple of the other; the graph is a straight line through (0, 0).
The amount of y for exactly 1 of x; the y-value of the point (1, r).
The point (0, 0) where the two axes meet.

worked_example_script.text: Build the table for apples at 3 dollars per pound: (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12). Plot the four points on a grid with pounds across and dollars up.
What shape do the dots make? Would the line pass through (0, 0)?
The dots sit on a straight line through the origin because every pound adds the same 3 dollars. The point (4, 12) says 4 pounds cost 12 dollars, and (1, 3) is the unit rate.
If a student reads (4, 12) as two unrelated numbers, have them label each number with its axis name before speaking.
Your turn: a walker goes 4 miles per hour. Plot three points and tell me what (2, 8) means.

practice_problems.stem: Oranges cost 2 dollars per pound. Complete the table: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, ?)
On a pounds vs dollars graph, what does the point (1, 2) tell you?
practice_problems.answer: 1 pound costs 2 dollars, the unit rate

practice_problems.stem: A printer prints 6 pages per minute. Plot the points for 1, 2, and 3 minutes and name them.
On the printer graph, what does the point (3, 18) mean?
practice_problems.answer: In 3 minutes the printer prints 18 pages

practice_problems.stem: Table: (2, 10), (4, 20), (6, 30). Is it proportional, and what is the unit rate?
practice_problems.answer: Yes, y is 5 times x every row, unit rate 5

practice_problems.stem: Why does the graph of a steady 8 miles per hour ride pass through (0, 0)?
practice_problems.answer: After 0 hours the rider has gone 0 miles

practice_problems.stem: Two workers: A's graph passes through (1, 12) and B's through (1, 15). Who earns more per hour, and how do their lines compare?
practice_problems.answer: B earns more, 15 dollars per hour vs 12, so B's line is steeper

practice_problems.stem: Kim looked at the point (4, 12) on the apples graph (3 dollars per pound). Find and fix her mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Kim swapped the variables. Pounds is on the x-axis and cost on the y-axis, so (4, 12) means 4 pounds cost 12 dollars. Check: 4 pounds times 3 dollars per pound is 12 dollars.

activities.title: Build the Line from the Deal
materials: Deal cards like '3 dollars per pound' and '8 miles per hour'
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a deal card and build its table with counters: 1 pound gets 3 counters, 2 pounds get 6, up to 5 pounds.
2. Plot each row as a point on grid paper with labeled axes.
3. Lay a ruler along the dots: they line up and aim at (0, 0). Say why 0 gives 0.
4. Pick any dot and say it as a sentence: this many pounds cost this many dollars.
5. Repeat with a second deal card and compare which line is steeper and why.

activities.title: Point, Meaning, Rate
materials: Card deck: point cards, meaning-sentence cards, unit rate cards
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each point card, like (4, 12) on the apples graph, to its meaning sentence and its unit rate card.
3. To claim a match, read the sentence aloud with the axis labels.
4. Two decoy meaning cards swap the variables; set them aside and explain the swap.

pairs.left: (4, 12) on apples at 3 dollars per pound
(1, 3) on apples at 3 dollars per pound
pairs.right: 1 pound costs 3 dollars, the unit rate

pairs.left: (2, 16) on a ride at 8 miles per hour
(3, 18) on a printer at 6 pages per minute

pairs.right: None of the first quantity gives none of the second

strategy_links.why: Building the table with counters and then plotting makes the point-as-one-fact idea concrete before the graph language is named.
Saying each point aloud as a sentence with axis labels makes the invisible reading order, x then y with their variables, audible and checkable.
The variable-swap misreading of a point is stable and baitable; find-and-fix items confront it directly.

questioning_prompts: What does the x-axis measure, and what does the y-axis measure?
Say the point (3, 9) as a sentence about the situation.
Which point shows the unit rate, and how do you know?
Why must the line pass through (0, 0)?
If the price per pound went up, what would happen to the line?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads a point's numbers without attaching them to the variables, or swaps them.
misconception_redirects.say: Touch the x-axis label, then the point's first number; touch the y-axis label, then the second number. Now say the sentence.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched each number to its axis, so the point told you a true fact.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student thinks any increasing table is proportional.
misconception_redirects.say: Check the rule row by row: is y always the same multiple of x? In (1, 4), (2, 7), (3, 10) it is not, so the points do not aim at (0, 0).
misconception_redirects.praise: You tested the multiply rule instead of just noticing it goes up, that is the real check.

quick_checks.prompt: Bananas cost 2 dollars per pound. What does (5, 10) mean on the graph?
quick_checks.look_for: 5 pounds cost 10 dollars, not 5 dollars for 10 pounds.

quick_checks.prompt: Which point on that graph shows the unit rate?

worked_solution.stem: Apples cost 3 dollars per pound. Graph the relationship and explain what the point (4, 12) means.
worked_solution.answer: The points lie on a straight line through (0, 0); (4, 12) means 4 pounds cost 12 dollars.

steps.annotation: Each pound adds 3 dollars, so multiply pounds by 3.

0 pounds cost 0 dollars, and the rate never changes.
Read x with its axis, then y with its axis, as one fact.

faded_example.answer: The points lie on a line through (0, 0); (3, 24) means 3 hours covers 24 miles.

steps.annotation: Each row becomes one point.
What shape do the dots make, and where does the line start?

skills.name: Describe a data set from a dot plot, including values that fall far from the rest

prerequisite_skill.description: Read a dot plot of one measured quantity and describe where the data bunches, how spread out it is, and whether any value sits far from the others.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Quiz scores on a dot plot bunch between 7 and 9, and one dot sits at 2. How would you describe the dot at 2?

skills.i_do_script: In grade 7 we described a whole data set from a dot plot, one dot per measurement. Watch this plot of minutes spent on homework: dots pile up over 20, 25, and 30, and one lone dot sits over 60. First I say where the data bunches: most students spent 20 to 30 minutes. Then I say how spread out it is: from 20 to 60, a range of 40. Last I name any stray value: the 60 sits far from the pile, so it stands apart from the rest of the data. Bunch, spread, stray: those three words describe almost any plot, and they are the same eyes we will use on scatter plots.

canonical_error.pattern: Calls the highest or lowest value a stray point even when it sits right next to the rest of the data
canonical_error.example: For dots at 20, 22, 24, 25, 26, 28 says '28 is way off by itself because it is the biggest'
canonical_error.why: A value stands apart only when there is a wide gap between it and the rest of the data. Being the maximum or minimum is not enough; the student must look for the gap, not the rank.

skills.item_template: A small dot plot described in text (values and counts, whole numbers). Student states where the data bunches, the range, or which value if any sits far from the rest. Short response.

sample_items.stem: Dots at 20, 22, 24, 25, 26, 28 and one dot at 60. Which value sits far from the rest?
sample_items.answer: 60, there is a wide gap between 28 and 60

sample_items.stem: Dots at 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9. Where does the data bunch?
sample_items.answer: Between 7 and 9, mostly at 8

sample_items.stem: Dots at 10, 12, 13, 15, 40. What is the range of the data?
Dots at 5, 6, 6, 7, 8. Is the 8 far from the rest of the data? Why or why not?
sample_items.answer: No, it sits right next to the 7, there is no wide gap

sample_items.stem: Dots at 2, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34. Which value stands apart?
sample_items.answer: 2, the rest bunch from 30 to 34

sample_items.stem: How many measurements does a dot plot with 12 dots show?
sample_items.answer: 12, one dot per measurement

sample_items.stem: Dots at 50, 52, 55, 55, 58, 60. Does any value sit far from the rest?
sample_items.answer: No, the values run close together from 50 to 60

sample_items.stem: Dots bunch from 15 to 20 with one dot at 45. Describe the data in one sentence.
sample_items.answer: Most values bunch between 15 and 20, and 45 sits far from the rest

redirect_script.stop: Is there a wide gap before that value, or is it just the biggest?
redirect_script.prompt: Slide your finger along the number line. A value stands apart only if you cross a wide empty stretch to reach it. Biggest is a rank; far away is a gap.
redirect_script.praise: You looked for the gap instead of the rank, that is how you spot a value that truly stands apart.

vocabulary.definition: A number line with one dot above it for each measurement in the data set.
The greatest value minus the least value; how wide the data spreads.
A stretch of the number line inside the data with no dots on it.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from 0 to 70. Stack dots at 20, 22, 24, 25, 26, 28 and one dot at 60.
Where do the dots pile up? Do you cross any wide empty stretch to reach a dot?
The data bunches from 20 to 28. Between 28 and 60 the line is empty, a wide gap, so the 60 stands far from the rest. The range is 60 - 20 = 40.
If a student says 28 stands apart because it is the biggest of the pile, have them trace from 26 to 28: no gap.
Your turn: dots at 5, 6, 6, 7, 8 and one at 25. Describe the bunch, the range, and any stray value.

practice_problems.stem: A dot plot has dots at 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5. Where does the data bunch?
practice_problems.answer: From 3 to 5, mostly at 4

practice_problems.stem: Dots at 10, 12, 14, 20. What is the range?
Dots at 15, 16, 16, 17, 18 and one dot at 40. Which value sits far from the rest, and how do you know?
practice_problems.answer: 40, there is a wide empty gap between 18 and 40

practice_problems.stem: Dots at 1, 25, 26, 27, 28. Which value stands apart? Does a stray value have to be the biggest?
practice_problems.answer: 1 stands apart; no, a stray value can be the smallest, it just needs a wide gap

practice_problems.stem: Dots at 30, 32, 33, 35, 36, 38. Does any value sit far from the rest?
practice_problems.answer: No, the values run close together with no wide gap

practice_problems.stem: Class quiz scores: dots bunch from 7 to 9 and one dot sits at 2. Describe the data in one sentence.
practice_problems.answer: Most scores bunch between 7 and 9, and the score of 2 sits far from the rest

practice_problems.stem: Make up 7 data values so the dots bunch between 40 and 45 and exactly one value stands far apart.
practice_problems.answer: Example: 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45, 70. Six values bunch from 40 to 45 and 70 sits past a wide gap

practice_problems.stem: Leo described the dot plot with dots at 20, 22, 24, 25, 26, 28. Find and fix his mistake.
shown_work: Leo wrote: '28 is the biggest value.'
practice_problems.answer: Leo used rank instead of a gap. 28 sits right next to 26, so nothing stands apart in this data. A value is far from the rest only when a wide empty stretch separates it.

activities.title: Sticky Dot Line
materials: Painter's tape number line on a table or wall
activities.instructions:
1. Read a data card, like minutes of homework: 20, 22, 24, 25, 26, 28, 60.
2. Place one sticky dot above the line for each value.
3. Put one hand over the bunch and slide a finger across any wide empty stretch to a lone dot.
4. Say the three-part description aloud: where it bunches, the range, any value that stands apart.
5. Repeat with a card that has no stray value and notice the description changes.

activities.title: Gap or Just the Biggest?
materials: Card set of small data lists
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each card into 'Has a value far from the rest' or 'All values run together.'
2. For each card, sketch the dots on a mini number line before sorting; the sort is judged by the picture.
3. Rule check: a stray value needs a wide gap, not just the top rank.
4. Debrief with a card whose biggest value is NOT a stray value and explain why.

skills.name: Identify the type of association shown by a scatter plot as positive, negative, or none
skills.i_do_script: Association is something you SEE -- read the cloud, not the list. The type of association is about DIRECTION: which way the dots drift as I read left to right. If y climbs as x increases, the dots drift up to the right -- a POSITIVE association. If y falls as x increases, the dots drift down to the right -- a NEGATIVE association. If the dots scatter with no up-or-down tendency, there is NO association. skills.name: Identify clustering and outliers in a scatter plot
skills.i_do_script: Picture the dots as kids on a playground: most stand together in a huddle, and sometimes one kid stands way off alone. The huddle and the loner get different names, and the picture tells you which is which. Besides direction and shape, I describe WHERE the points sit. CLUSTERING is when several points bunch tightly together in a group. An OUTLIER is a single point that sits far away from all the others. Watch (1, 10), (2, 12), (3, 11), (4, 13), (20, 80): four of the points are bunched near x = 1 to 4 with y around 10 to 13 -- that bunch is a cluster. The point (20, 80) sits way off by itself -- that lonely point is an outlier. The key difference: a cluster is MANY points close together; an outlier is ONE point far from the rest.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses clustering with outliers -- labels a single far-off point a 'cluster,' or calls a tight bunch of points 'outliers'

canonical_error.why: Clustering means several points bunched close together; an outlier means one point far from all the others. A cluster is a group of many points; an outlier is a single lonely point. Swapping the two labels describes the plot backwards.

Watch (1, 20), (2, 30), (3, 42), (4, 55), (5, 66), (20, 15): the bulk of the points climb by about 10 each step, so it's positive and roughly linear -- but (20, 15) sits far below that rising pattern, so there's an outlier too. My description: 'a positive, linear association with an outlier.' One label alone would be incomplete.

canonical_error.pattern: Names only one characteristic -- usually the direction -- and stops, ignoring the plot's other features like form or an outlier
canonical_error.example: For (1, 15), (2, 26), (3, 38), (4, 50), (5, 61), (18, 12) the student says only 'positive association' and never mentions that the bulk is roughly linear or that (18, 12) is an outlier
canonical_error.why: The standard asks students to identify MULTIPLE characteristics at once. A complete description reports direction AND form, and flags any cluster or outlier; naming a single feature under-describes the plot.

skills.item_template: A short list of (x, y) pairs, usually with a clear trend plus an outlier, given in text. Student names two or more characteristics. Multiple choice (select two) or short response. (No figure needed.)

sample_items.answer: A positive, linear association (the bulk) AND an outlier at (20, 15).

sample_items.answer: A positive association that is nonlinear -- the steps +3, +6, +10, +15 keep growing.
Negative and linear -- y falls by about 20 each step.

sample_items.answer: Negative and linear, with the points clustered along the line and no outliers.

redirect_script.prompt: Run the whole checklist: direction (positive/negative/none), then form (linear/nonlinear), then features (any cluster or outlier). Give at least two of them for a complete description.
redirect_script.praise: You reported the direction AND the form (and the outlier) -- that's a full description, not just one label.

Whether the association is positive, negative, or none.
The overall relationship a scatter plot shows between the two variables.

skills.name: Construct a scatter plot from a table and interpret the pattern in context
skills.i_do_script: Here I turn a data table into a plot and then say what it means using the REAL variable names. The first column is x (the explanatory variable) and the second is y (the response). Watch a table of temperature (F) and bottled waters sold: (60, 15), (70, 22), (80, 30), (90, 41), (100, 52). I plot each pair, then read the direction: as temperature goes up, sales go up, so it's a positive association. In context: 'As temperature increases, the number of waters sold increases.' The key move is to track the RESPONSE variable as the explanatory variable grows -- and to say it in the story's own words.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads the contextual direction backwards -- reports the response variable increasing when the plot shows it decreasing (or the reverse) as x increases
canonical_error.example: For a plot of years (x) versus town population (y) whose dots fall from left to right, the student completes 'As time increased, the population INCREASED,' when the points show population decreasing
canonical_error.why: Interpreting in context means tracking the response variable's direction as x grows. Falling dots mean y DECREASES as x increases -- a negative association -- so the contextual sentence must say 'decreased.' Naming the wrong direction misreports the relationship.

skills.item_template: A data table (given as text pairs) with named variables. Student states the association and completes an in-context sentence, or plots the points. Multiple part (construct + interpret). (Data shown as a table/pairs in text; no scatter figure invented.)

sample_items.stem: Temperature (F) vs bottled waters sold: (60, 15), (70, 22), (80, 30), (90, 41), (100, 52). Complete: 'As temperature increases, sales ___.' What is the association?
sample_items.answer: increase; a positive association.

sample_items.stem: Years since 2000 vs town population (hundreds): (0, 50), (5, 44), (10, 38), (15, 30), (20, 22). Complete: 'As time increased, the population ___.'
sample_items.answer: decreased -- a negative association.

sample_items.stem: Miles driven vs gas remaining (gal): (0, 12), (50, 10), (100, 7), (150, 5), (200, 2). Describe the pattern in context.
sample_items.answer: Negative: as miles driven increase, gas remaining decreases (roughly linear).

sample_items.stem: Hours studied vs test score: (1, 55), (2, 62), (3, 70), (4, 78), (5, 85). Interpret the pattern in context.
sample_items.answer: Positive: as hours studied increase, test scores increase (roughly linear).

redirect_script.stop: Do the dots go up or down as you read right?
redirect_script.prompt: Track the response variable as x increases: if the dots fall, the response DECREASES; if they rise, it INCREASES. Then fill the in-context sentence to match the direction of the dots.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the sentence to the direction of the dots -- that's interpreting in context correctly.

vocabulary.definition: Plot the (x, y) pairs from a data table to make a scatter plot.
Describe the pattern using the real variable names and what they mean.
Stated in terms of the actual quantities, such as temperature and sales.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'Hours of daylight vs ice-cream sales: (10, 20), (12, 28), (14, 35), (16, 44). Interpret in context.'
As the hours of daylight increase, what do the sales do?
Sales go 20, 28, 35, 44 as daylight increases -- they rise. In context: as daylight hours increase, ice-cream sales increase. That's a positive association.
If a student writes 'sales decrease,' ask 'are the sales numbers getting bigger or smaller as daylight goes up?'
Your turn: temperature vs hot-cocoa sales (30, 50), (40, 40), (50, 30), (60, 20) -- interpret in context.

practice_problems.stem: When you plot a table of (temperature, sales) pairs, which value goes on the x-axis?
practice_problems.answer: The first/explanatory variable -- temperature goes on the x-axis, sales on the y-axis.

practice_problems.stem: A plot of hours studied vs test score drifts upward. Complete: 'As hours studied increase, test scores ___.'
practice_problems.answer: increase (a positive association).

practice_problems.stem: Temperature (F) vs bottled waters sold: (60, 15), (70, 22), (80, 30), (90, 41), (100, 52). Describe the pattern in context.
practice_problems.answer: Positive association: as temperature increases, water sales increase (roughly linear).

practice_problems.answer: decreased -- a negative association.

practice_problems.stem: A store tracked temperature (F) and hot-cocoa cups sold: (30, 50), (40, 42), (50, 33), (60, 25), (70, 16). Jo interpreted it. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Jo wrote: 'The dots on my plot go down from left to right.'
'So as temperature increases, cocoa sales INCREASE.'
practice_problems.answer: Jo read the direction backwards. Falling dots mean the response DECREASES as x increases: as temperature increases, cocoa sales DECREASE. It is a negative association.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: reading the contextual direction backwards.

practice_problems.stem: Plot these and describe: miles driven vs gas remaining (gal): (0, 12), (50, 10), (100, 7), (150, 5), (200, 2). What is the association, in context?
practice_problems.answer: Negative: as miles driven increase, gas remaining decreases (roughly linear).

practice_problems.stem: Make a small table (5 pairs) for 'practice hours vs free-throw %' that shows a positive association, then interpret it in context.
practice_problems.answer: Example: (1, 40), (2, 48), (3, 55), (4, 63), (5, 70). As practice hours increase, free-throw percentage increases -- a positive association.

practice_problems.stem: A plot of 'shoe size vs test score' shows dots scattered with no upward or downward drift. Write the correct in-context interpretation.
practice_problems.answer: There is no association: as shoe size increases, test scores do not consistently increase or decrease.

activities.title: Plot It, Then Say It
activities.instructions:
1. Take a table card, label the x-axis with the first variable and the y-axis with the second.
2. Plot every pair to build the scatter plot.
3. Read the direction of the dots and fill the sentence frame: 'As ___ increases, ___ ___.'
4. Debrief: swap plots with another pair and check that their sentence matches the direction of their dots.

activities.title: Which Way Do the Dots Really Go?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Jo's claim that falling dots mean 'sales increase' for temperature vs cocoa sales.
2. List the sales values in order of temperature and draw an arrow for their direction.
3. The arrow points down, so fix the sentence to say 'decrease.'
4. Write the rule: the in-context sentence must match the direction of the dots.

content.error_step: Jo named the wrong direction -- the dots fall, but Jo wrote 'increase.'

A math-journal sentence in the variables' own words consolidates 'interpret in context' as a writing habit.

skills.name: Analyze and critique claims about association, and build a plot to match descriptors
skills.i_do_script: At the top of this standard I ARGUE about scatter plots: I judge whether a described pattern really matches the data, I build a plot to fit given descriptors, and I refuse to jump from 'these move together' to 'one causes the other.' Watch a claim: a plot shows a strong positive association between the number of firefighters sent to a fire and the damage caused, and a student says 'more firefighters CAUSE more damage.' The plot really does show a positive association -- but a scatter plot shows only that two things move TOGETHER, never that one causes the other. A hidden variable, the fire's SIZE, drives both. So the honest description is 'a positive association,' and the causal claim is not justified.

canonical_error.pattern: Concludes that because two variables show an association, one must CAUSE the other -- treating correlation as causation
canonical_error.example: A positive association between ice-cream sales (x) and sunburns (y) leads the student to claim 'buying ice cream causes sunburns,' ignoring that hot, sunny weather drives both
canonical_error.why: An association shows the variables move together, not that one produces the other. A hidden (confounding) variable can drive both, so a scatter plot alone can describe a pattern but cannot establish causation.

skills.item_template: A described scatter plot (as text pairs or a described pattern) plus a claim, or a set of descriptors to build a plot for. Student critiques the claim, repairs a description, or lists points matching descriptors. Multiple-part short response. (No scatter figure invented; data shown as text pairs.)

sample_items.stem: A plot shows a strong positive association between the number of firefighters at a fire and the damage caused. A student says 'more firefighters cause more damage.' Is the claim justified?
sample_items.answer: No. A scatter plot shows association, not causation. Bigger fires cause both more firefighters AND more damage.

sample_items.stem: Create a set of (x, y) pairs (at least 6 points) with a negative, linear association and one outlier. List them.
A person's plot rises and then bends upward more steeply, and they call it 'positive, linear.' Correct the description.
sample_items.answer: The direction (positive) is right, but the form is wrong: a bending path is nonlinear. It is a positive, nonlinear association.

sample_items.stem: True or false: a scatter plot with a positive association proves that x causes y.
sample_items.answer: False -- association does not prove causation.

redirect_script.stop: Move together, or one CAUSES the other -- which does the plot show?
redirect_script.prompt: A scatter plot can only show that two things move together. Before claiming cause, ask 'could a hidden variable explain both?' If yes, say the variables are associated, not that one causes the other.
redirect_script.praise: You named the pattern as an association and questioned the cause -- that's honest analysis.

vocabulary.definition: An association means two variables move together; causation means one makes the other change -- a scatter plot shows only association.
A hidden third variable that influences both plotted variables.
Judge whether a claim about the data is justified and explain why or why not.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for line of best fit, bivariate patterns, and two-way tables (8.DSP.2-4, AI.DS.4).

worked_example_script.text: Write 'Positive association between hours of TV and shoe size in kids. Claim: watching TV grows your feet.'
Is there really a cause here, or could something else explain both?
Older kids watch more TV AND have bigger feet -- AGE drives both. The plot shows an association, but TV does not cause bigger feet. Correlation is not causation.
If a student accepts the causal claim, ask 'what hidden variable could be behind both?'
Your turn: critique 'more lifeguards on duty causes more drownings' when the two are positively associated.

practice_problems.stem: True or false: if two variables have a positive association, then one must cause the other.
practice_problems.answer: False -- association is not the same as causation.

practice_problems.stem: Rewrite as a NON-causal statement: 'More firefighters cause more fire damage.'
practice_problems.answer: 'Fires with more firefighters tend to have more damage' -- they are associated, but a bigger fire drives both.

practice_problems.stem: A plot shows a strong positive association between ice-cream sales and sunburns. A student says 'ice cream causes sunburns.' Is the claim justified?
practice_problems.answer: No -- hot, sunny weather increases both ice-cream sales and sunburns. The association does not prove ice cream causes sunburns.

practice_problems.stem: Create a set of (x, y) pairs (at least 6 points) with a negative, linear association and one outlier. List them.
practice_problems.answer: Example: (1, 60), (2, 52), (3, 45), (4, 38), (5, 30), (6, 22) with an outlier at (3, 5). The bulk falls by about 8 each step; (3, 5) sits far below.

practice_problems.stem: A person made a scatter plot and wrote a description. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: They wrote: 'This shows that increasing x CAUSES y to drop.'
practice_problems.answer: The data does show a negative association (y falls as x rises), but a scatter plot cannot prove CAUSATION. The correct description is 'a negative, linear association,' not a cause-and-effect claim -- some other factor may drive both.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: sliding from association to causation.

practice_problems.stem: A person's plot rises and then bends upward more steeply. They call it 'positive, linear.' Critique and correct the description.
practice_problems.answer: The direction is right (positive), but the form is wrong: a bending path is nonlinear. The correct description is 'positive, nonlinear.'
practice_problems.notes: Critique a described pattern (matches the Above band).

practice_problems.stem: Create a scatter-plot description (a list of points) that a classmate must critique: include one true feature and one that is easy to over-claim as causation.
practice_problems.answer: Example: (1, 5), (2, 9), (3, 14), (4, 20), (5, 27) for 'hours of daylight vs ice-cream sales' -- a positive association, but claiming daylight CAUSES the sales ignores temperature as a hidden driver.

practice_problems.stem: Two variables show NO association. A student concludes 'so one prevents the other.' What is wrong with that?
practice_problems.answer: No association means the variables do not move together at all -- it gives no evidence that one prevents (or causes) the other. No pattern means no such conclusion.

activities.title: Justified or Overclaiming?
materials: Claim cards pairing a described plot with a statement
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each card into 'Justified description' or 'Overclaims causation.'
2. For each 'overclaims' card, name a hidden variable that could explain both.
3. Rewrite each overclaiming card as a 'tend to move together' statement.
4. Debrief: which words (causes, makes, because of) are red flags on a scatter plot?

cards.text: Positive plot: 'x and y tend to increase together.'
Positive plot: 'x causes y to increase.'
Ice cream & sunburns rise together: 'ice cream causes sunburns.'
Negative plot: 'as x increases, y tends to decrease.'
Firefighters & damage rise together: 'more firefighters cause more damage.'
Curved rising plot: 'this is a positive, nonlinear association.'

activities.title: Correlation Is Not Causation
activities.instructions:
1. Read the claim that a negative association between x and y proves 'x causes y to drop.'
2. Underline the cause word and ask: does the plot show cause, or just that they move together?
3. Name a hidden variable that could drive both.
4. Rewrite the description without a cause claim, and write the rule: a scatter plot shows association, not causation.

content.worked_problem: (1, 90), (2, 72), (3, 58), (4, 40), (5, 25). Claim: 'increasing x CAUSES y to drop.'
content.error_step: The claim reads a negative association as proof of cause and effect.
content.why: The plot shows y falls as x rises -- a negative association -- but a scatter plot cannot prove causation; a hidden variable may drive both.

strategy_links.why: The correlation-implies-causation leap is a precise, baitable error; find-and-fix that hunts for a hidden variable corrects it.
A math-journal entry justifying or critiquing a claim builds the argument habit the standard tops out on.
Think-pair-share debating 'is this claim justified?' forces students to defend or critique inferences aloud with the data as evidence.

What hidden variable could explain both of these at once?
Is the described pattern (direction and form) actually correct for this data?
How would you rewrite the claim so it is justified by the plot?
Does your created plot match every descriptor -- direction, form, and each feature?

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4, describing more than one characteristic of a scatter plot at once, the Approaching-to-At hinge. If they pass, move up to S5 (construct and interpret in context) and S6 (critique and build to match descriptors). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks whether the student can graph a proportional relationship and read a point as one fact in context, and B2 checks whether they can describe a dot plot's bunch, spread, and stray values, the two grade 7 habits scatter plot description leans on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (plotting ordered pairs, grade 5) and F2 (reading how one quantity changes with another in a table, grade 6) locate the gap. S1, S2, and S3 remain available to probe the standard's own direction, form, and cluster-outlier judgments.
